About

Who built this, and why.

I am Paula Silva, Developer Solutions Advisor and Software Latam Leader on the Data & AI team, Global Black Belt for Microsoft Americas. My work spans the full AI transformation journey, from application and legacy modernization to agentic architecture and platform engineering, helping enterprise teams adopt AI-assisted development at scale. Hooks are where an agent stops being a black box and becomes a system you can govern.

This deck is the technical deep dive on GitHub Copilot hooks, rebuilt for the September 2026 hooks reference: the fourteen lifecycle events and their exact input and output contracts, exit codes and fail-open versus fail-closed rules, matchers and the Claude-compatible format, where hooks live and in what order they load, what the cloud agent, VS Code, JetBrains and the GitHub Copilot SDK support, guardrails against destructive commands and prompt injection, quality automation, audit to a SIEM through HTTP hooks, OpenTelemetry, policy hooks and managed settings, and an adoption path with a starter kit and a lab.

It is built as a two to three hour workshop for platform and security engineers and for the developers who will write the first hooks: every part closes with a how-to with real JSON and a scenarios slide, there is a hook decision simulator you run live, and the last part hands the room a ninety day path. Every fact is checked against docs.github.com, the GitHub Copilot CLI changelog and the VS Code docs as of September 2026.

Vocabulary

Sixteen terms the whole room needs before slide seven.

Hook
A command, HTTP call or prompt the runtime executes at a lifecycle event, with a JSON payload in and an optional JSON decision out.
Event
One of fourteen moments in a session: sessionStart to sessionEnd, prompt, tool, subagent, compaction, error, notification.
preToolUse
Fires before a tool runs; the only event that can deny a call, with permissionDecision allow, deny or ask.
agentStop
Fires when the agent wants to end the turn; block forces another turn with your reason as the prompt; eight blocks maximum.
Matcher
A regex compiled as ^(?:PATTERN)$ against the tool name, agent name, trigger or notification type.
PascalCase alias
Stop, PreToolUse, UserPromptSubmit: Claude and VS Code compatible names that switch the payload to snake_case.
Fail-closed
A crashed command hook on preToolUse denies the tool. Timeouts never do: they always fail open.
Policy hook
Admin-installed in policy.d or the registry; loads first, cannot be disabled, CLI only.
disableAllHooks
The documented switch: in a hooks file it skips that file, in the repository settings.json it skips every non‑policy hook.
additionalContext
Text a hook injects into the session: at start, after a tool, before a subagent. Capped at 10 KB after a tool.
stop_hook_active
True when the current turn was already forced by a block; the field that lets your agentStop hook stop itself.
http hook
POSTs the payload to an https endpoint; fail-open; the way to keep evidence out of an ephemeral cloud sandbox.
Permission rule
Kind(argument) patterns like shell(git:*), read(.env), MyMCP(create_issue); deny beats allow, even with ‑‑allow‑all.
Sandbox bypass
A tool asking to run outside the sandbox; a hook can deny it but never pre‑approve it.
Managed settings
MDM or server-managed JSON with allowManagedHooksOnly and strictPluginOnlyCustomization; most restrictive wins.
Safe output
The Agentic Workflows equivalent of a guardrail: the agent proposes, a scoped job writes, threat detection scans first.
Watch outHooks are not permissions and not a sandbox. Permissions decide what the agent may call, the sandbox limits what a call can reach, hooks are code you run in between with a payload and a decision. The three compose; the deck keeps them apart.

Why hooks

Permissions answer may it. Hooks answer what happens when it does.

Permissions and the sandbox

Permission rules say which tools and arguments the agent may use; the sandbox limits what a call can reach on the machine. Both are declarative and both are blind to context: they cannot read the payload, log it, transform it or decide by time of day.

Hooks

Code you own, run by the runtime at fourteen moments with the full payload: the command about to run, the prompt just typed, the result just produced, the reason the agent wants to stop. It can deny, modify, inject context, notify or ship evidence elsewhere.

Two surfaces, one formatThe GitHub Copilot CLI runs every event; the cloud agent runs a subset in its Linux sandbox. Same configuration, same payloads.
Claude compatiblePascalCase names, snake_case payloads and .claude/settings.json are read, so one hooks file can serve GitHub Copilot, VS Code and Claude Code.
Enterprise gradePolicy hooks load first and cannot be disabled; managed settings can allow only managed hooks; every hook emits OpenTelemetry span events.
Watch outA hook can edit the agent's behavior, and the agent can edit the hook script. In VS Code use chat.tools.edits.autoApprove to require approval on hook script edits; in the CLI keep hook scripts under a path the deny rules protect.

What fires when, what it can do, and what it returns.

Scene · the contract

A payload goes in on stdin. A decision comes out on stdout.

stdin is the whole storyEvent, session id, tool name and the raw toolArgs string arrive as one JSON object. Parse it twice: the object, then the command inside.
stdout is the decisionOne JSON object, nothing else. permissionDecision plus a reason the agent can act on; progress lines are stripped, two objects are ignored.
Exit codes carry meaningExit 0 parses stdout; exit 2 is a deny on the gates; other errors fail open, except preToolUse. Timeouts always fail open.

How to · the configuration file

version, hooks, event, entries. Three types, ten fields.

A hooks file is a JSON object with version 1 and a hooks object keyed by event. Each event holds an array of entries that run in order; the same event in several sources runs all entries. Types are command, the default, http and prompt. Command entries take bash, powershell or command as a cross-platform fallback, exec with args for no shell, cwd, env, and timeoutSec, default 30.

.github/hooks/policy.json
{  "version": 1,  "hooks": {    "sessionStart": [{ "type": "prompt", "prompt": "/context" }],    "preToolUse": [      { "type": "command", "matcher": "bash|powershell",        "bash": "./scripts/pre-tool-policy.sh", "powershell": "./scripts/pre-tool-policy.ps1",        "cwd": ".github/hooks", "timeoutSec": 15 },      { "type": "http", "url": "https://hooks.example.com/copilot",        "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer $HOOKS_TOKEN" }, "allowedEnvVars": ["HOOKS_TOKEN"] }    ],    "postToolUse": [{ "type": "command", "bash": "cat >> logs/tool-results.jsonl" }],    "sessionEnd": [{ "type": "command", "exec": "./scripts/cleanup", "args": ["--quiet"], "timeoutSec": 60 }]  }}
http
url, headers, allowedEnvVars to expand variables in headers, timeoutSec. https only; localhost needs COPILOT_HOOK_ALLOW_LOCALHOST=1; preToolUse and permissionRequest must be https.
prompt
prompt text or a slash command, sessionStart only, CLI only, new interactive sessions; not on resume, not in -p, may not fire in the cloud.

The contracts

Input and output per event, as the reference writes them.

Event Input fields Output fields
sessionStartsource, initialPromptadditionalContext
userPromptSubmittedpromptmodifiedPrompt (SDK only), responseContent to answer without the model
preToolUsetoolName, toolArgs as a JSON string; tool_name and tool_input in PascalCasepermissionDecision, permissionDecisionReason, modifiedArgs, additionalContext
postToolUsetoolName, toolArgs, toolResult with resultType and textResultForLlmmodifiedResult, additionalContext; a failure result routes to postToolUseFailure
postToolUseFailuretoolName, toolArgs, erroradditionalContext; exit 2 stdout appended
agentStoptranscriptPath, stopReason end_turn, stop_hook_activedecision block or allow, reason used as the next prompt
subagentStart · StopagentName, transcriptPath; agentId, agentType, responseadditionalContext; decision, reason, modifiedResponse
permissionRequestthe permission being requestedbehavior allow or deny, message, interrupt
preCompact · errorOccurredtrigger, customInstructions; error, errorContext, recoverablenone
notificationmessage, title, notification_typeadditionalContext as a user message
Watch outtoolArgs arrives as a string you parse, not an object: jq -r '.toolArgs' then jq -r '.command'. Half of the broken hooks in the wild are a missing second parse. The PascalCase form gives you tool_input already parsed when possible.

Exit codes and failure

What the runtime does when your hook returns, crashes, or never returns.

01
Exit 0
Success; stdout is parsed as one JSON object. Progress lines of the form {"type":"progress"} are stripped first; two decision objects make invalid JSON and are ignored. Output capped at 10 MiB.
02
Exit 2
A warning by default, stderr shown. On preToolUse and permissionRequest it is a deny even if stdout says allow. On postToolUseFailure the stdout becomes additionalContext.
03
Other non-zero
Logged, the run continues, fail-open, with one exception: preToolUse is fail-closed and the tool is denied with the reason hook errored.
04
Timeout
Always fail-open, every event, even policy hooks. The process is killed after timeoutSec, a warning is logged, and the tool proceeds through the normal permission flow. Keep guardrails fast.
05
HTTP hooks
Fail-open on network error, timeout or a non-2xx, including preToolUse. If the guardrail must hold when the network is down, it is a command hook, not an HTTP hook.
Watch outSay it twice in the room: a slow guardrail is no guardrail. A preToolUse policy that calls a remote service has to answer inside timeoutSec, or it silently allows.
function binarySearch(a, x) {
  let lo = 0, hi = a.length - 1;
  while (lo <= hi) {
    const mid = (lo + hi) >> 1;
    if (a[mid] === x) return mid;
    a[mid] < x ? lo = mid + 1 : hi = mid - 1;
  }
  return -1;
}

Matchers and names

Two matcher dialects, one regex rule, one tool‑name mapping.

matcher is a regex compiled as ^(?:PATTERN)$ and must match the whole value: toolName for preToolUse, postToolUse and permissionRequest; agentName for subagentStart; trigger for preCompact; notification_type for notification. An invalid regex skips the entry.
For PreToolUse and PermissionRequest the Claude dialect applies: *, ** or empty match all; a literal alternation like Bash or Edit|Write matches the runtime or Claude name; anything else is a regex against the Claude name. The payload switches to snake_case with tool_name and tool_input.
Name mappingbash and powershell become Bash; view is Read; create is Write; edit, str_replace_editor and apply_patch are Edit; grep and rg are Grep; glob is Glob; web_fetch and web_search are WebFetch and WebSearch; task is Agent.
MCP toolsNo documented naming convention for MCP tools in matchers. Gate MCP calls with permission rules like MyMCP(create_issue), and with preMcpToolCall in the SDK.
VS CodeParses matchers and ignores them; tool names differ: runTerminalCommand, editFiles, createFile. Branch on the payload inside the script instead.
Watch outA matcher narrows when the hook runs; the script still validates the payload. Never trust a matcher alone for a deny, because the same file may be read by a surface that ignores it.

How to · test a hook locally

Pipe a payload, read the JSON, check /env.

terminal · test the guardrail
Hook configurations load when the CLI starts, so restart after editing. /env lists hook counts and sources. Feed a hand-written payload through the script with echo and a pipe, compact the output with jq -c or ConvertTo-Json -Compress, and debug with set -x and a copy of stdin to stderr. Test the deny path with the harmless demo marker first.
Payload shape
timestamp in epoch milliseconds, cwd, toolName, toolArgs as a string. The tutorial's demo rule denies COPILOT_HOOKS_DENY_DEMO so you can prove the path without risk.
Cloud check
Push to the default branch, open a task, read the session log: hook output appears in the tool call group; hook.start and hook.end events appear in OpenTelemetry.



#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
INPUT=$(cat)
TOOL=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.toolName')
[ "$TOOL" = bash ] || exit 0
case "$CMD" in *sudo*) deny "no privilege escalation";; esac

SELECT tenant_id, count(*) AS runs,
       percentile_cont(0.95)
         WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY latency_ms)
FROM hook_events
WHERE fired_at > now() - interval '7 days'
GROUP BY tenant_id;

Scenarios
Four first hooks that teach the contract in an afternoon.
1
The session banner
sessionStart prints the branch, the node version and the state folder into additionalContext. Cheapest hook, immediately visible, teaches injection.
2
The tool log
postToolUse appends the payload to logs/tool-results.jsonl, the sample from the docs. Teaches payload shape and the 10 KB additionalContext cap.
3
The demo deny
preToolUse denies a marker string with a reason. Teaches permissionDecision, exit codes and the second parse of toolArgs.
4
The finish line
agentStop blocks once if tests did not run, then lets go using stop_hook_active. Teaches the forced turn and the eight‑block cap.
Watch outShip the four in one repository under .github/hooks and let every developer run copilot in it before writing their own. The contract is easier to read in a working file than in a table.

fn merge(a: &[i32], b: &[i32]) -> Vec<i32> {
    let (mut i, mut j) = (0, 0);
    let mut out = Vec::with_capacity(a.len() + b.len());
    while i < a.len() && j < b.len() {
        if a[i] <= b[j] { out.push(a[i]); i += 1 }
        else { out.push(b[j]); j += 1 }
    }
    out
}

Scene · the sources
Six files, one merged configuration, always in this order.
Policy loads firstpolicy.d and the registry are root-owned, load before trust is evaluated and ignore disableAllHooks. That is the admin lane.
Repo and user merge.github/hooks, ~/.copilot/hooks and the two settings.json all contribute; the repository overrides the user per key, nothing is replaced wholesale.
Plugins close the listPlugin hooks load last and can be forced or blocked by managed settings. The cloud agent reads only the repository file.

Folder trust
Trust is the first gate.

The cloud agent
Same contract, a narrower runtime. Seven rules to remember.
One source
.github/hooks/*.json on the default branch, cloned into the sandbox. No user files, no settings.json, no config.json, no plugins, no policy hooks.
bash only
Only bash and command entries run; cwd is /workspace; the file system is ephemeral, so evidence must leave through an http hook to an allow‑listed host.
Events
Everything except notification and permissionRequest. sessionStart once as new; userPromptSubmitted at most once; preCompact only auto; agentStop blocks count against the job timeout.
ask is deny
Non-interactive: a preToolUse ask becomes deny, all tools are pre-approved otherwise, and the firewall allows only GitHub and GitHub Copilot hosts unless an admin adds a rule.
Environment
GITHUB_COPILOT_API_TOKEN, GITHUB_COPILOT_GIT_TOKEN, COPILOT_AGENT_PROMPT and HOME=/root are set; GITHUB_TOKEN is not. Session id and cwd arrive in the stdin JSON.
Watch outThe cloud agent is where hooks matter most and where they are easiest to forget: no /env, no prompt to remind you. Put the guardrail file on the default branch before you enable the policy.

VS Code and JetBrains
The IDEs read the same files and speak a slightly different dialect.
Eight events: SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PreCompact, SubagentStart, SubagentStop, Stop. Reads .github/hooks, .claude/settings.json, ~/.copilot/hooks and agent frontmatter with chat.useCustomAgentHooks. Output uses continue, stopReason, systemMessage and hookSpecificOutput; exit 2 is a blocking error; most restrictive wins. Commands /hooks and /create-hook; policies ChatHooks and ChatAllowManagedHooksOnly.
Since March 11, 2026: hooks in .github/hooks/.json with four events, userPromptSubmitted, preToolUse, postToolUse and errorOccurred. Enough for a guardrail and a log; not enough for agentStop enforcement, which stays with the CLI and the cloud agent.
TranslationVS Code maps camelCase to PascalCase, bash to osx and linux, powershell to windows; entries also accept windows, linux and osx keys and a timeout of 30 seconds.
Tool namesrunTerminalCommand, editFiles, createFile, replace_string_in_file; tool_input is camelCase. Write the script to branch on both name sets.
SafetyThe agent can edit its own hook scripts; set chat.tools.edits.autoApprove to require approval on those paths.
Watch outPreview in the IDEs means the output shapes can still move. Keep the decision logic in the script and the IDE-specific output as a thin wrapper at the end.

How to · hooks in the GitHub Copilot SDK
Callbacks instead of files: the same events as functions in your language.
agent.ts · session hooks
const session = await client.createSession({  model: auto,  hooks: {    onSessionStart: async () => ({ additionalContext: Ticket 4471. State in ./state/. }),    onUserPromptSubmitted: async ({ prompt }) =>      injection.test(prompt) ? { responseContent: Rejected: instruction override. } : { modifiedPrompt: redact(prompt) },    onPreToolUse: async ({ toolName, toolArgs }) =>      toolName === bash && /rm -rf \//.test(toolArgs.command)        ? { permissionDecision: deny, permissionDecisionReason: Use a scoped path. }        : { permissionDecision: allow },    onPostToolUse: async ({ toolResult }) => ({ additionalContext: coverage.summary() }),    onPreMcpToolCall: async ({ serverName, meta }) => ({ meta: { ...meta, tenant: br-south } }),  },  onPermissionRequest: (r) => r.kind === shell ? { kind: approve-once } : deny,});
The SDK gives you the same events as functions, plus an onPermissionRequest handler, in Node, Python, Go, .NET, Java and Rust. Only here is modifiedPrompt honored, and only here does preMcpToolCall edit the _meta of an outgoing MCP call.
Outputs
preToolUse returns permissionDecision, permissionDecisionReason, modifiedArgs, additionalContext and suppressOutput; postToolUse returns modifiedResult, additionalContext, suppressOutput.
Governance
File hooks still load through the CLI runtime under the SDK, so policy hooks and managed settings apply to your product too.

Scenarios
Where the source decides the design.
01
Cloud-first team
All guardrails in .github/hooks on main, bash only, evidence through an http hook to the SIEM. The same file protects the CLI on laptops.
02
Regulated desktop
Policy hooks in policy.d, root-owned, plus allowManagedHooksOnly in MDM settings. Developers keep their own hooks for convenience, never for policy.
03
Multi-tool shop
One .claude/settings.json with PascalCase events serves Claude Code, VS Code and the GitHub Copilot CLI. Scripts branch on tool_name.
04
Internal product
SDK callbacks enforce product rules and hand telemetry to the app's tracer; file hooks from the platform team still apply underneath.
Watch outDecide the owner of each source before writing the first script. A guardrail the developer can edit is a convenience; a guardrail only the admin can edit is a control.

Scene · the gate
Two commands reach preToolUse. One passes. One comes back with a reason.
allow is silentnpm test matches nothing in the deny list; the hook exits 0 with allow and the runtime moves on to the permission service.
deny bounces with a reasonThe destructive delete never runs. The reason goes back to the model as the next instruction, so it proposes a scoped path instead of retrying.
preToolUse is fail-closedA crashed hook here denies the tool; a timeout does not. Keep the script local, under a second, and free of network calls.

How to · the destructive command guard
A preToolUse script with jq: parse twice, match, deny with a reason.
The tutorial layout: .github/hooks/copilot-cli-policy.json with cwd .github/hooks, scripts pre-tool-policy.sh and .ps1, a gitignored logs/audit.jsonl. Enforce only when toolName is bash. Rules from the docs: sudo, su and runas; rm -rf on the root; mkfs, dd and format; curl or wget piped into a shell; git push --force to main. Redact tokens before logging: ghp_, gho_, ghu_, ghs_, Bearer, ‑‑password, ‑‑token.
.github/hooks/scripts/pre-tool-policy.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bashINPUT=$(cat); TOOL=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.toolName // empty')[ "$TOOL" = bash ] || exit 0                        # enforce only on shellARGS=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.toolArgs // empty')   # first parse: a stringCMD=$(echo "$ARGS" | jq -r '.command // empty')     # second parse: the commanddeny() { jq -n --arg r "$1" '{permissionDecision:"deny", permissionDecisionReason:$r}'; exit 0; }case "$CMD" in  *sudo*|*runas*)                  deny "Privilege escalation is not allowed. Ask a human." ;;  *rm\ -rf\ /*)                    deny "Destructive delete. Use a scoped path." ;;  *mkfs*|*\ dd\ *|*format*)        deny "Disk operations are out of scope." ;;  *curl*\|*sh*|*wget*\|*sh*)       deny "Piping downloads into a shell is blocked." ;;  *git\ push*--force*main*)        deny "No force push to main. Open a pull request." ;;  *COPILOT_HOOKS_DENY_DEMO*)       deny "Demo rule fired." ;;esacecho "$CMD" | sed -E 's/(ghp|gho|ghu|ghs)_[A-Za-z0-9]+/[REDACTED]/g; s/(Bearer|--password|--token)[= ]\S+/\1 [REDACTED]/g' >> ../../logs/audit.jsonlexit 0
Deny shapejq -n --arg r "$reason" '{permissionDecision:"deny", permissionDecisionReason:$r}' then exit 0. The reason is shown to the agent, so write it as an instruction.
Fail-closedA crash is a deny on preToolUse; a timeout is not. Keep the script under a second and avoid network calls in the deny path.
Parse twicetoolArgs arrives as a string: jq -r .toolArgs, then jq -r .command. The second parse is where half of the broken hooks fail.

Three controls
Permissions, hooks and the sandbox: what each stops, and where.
ControlWhat it stopsWhereBlind spot
Permission rulestool kinds and argument patterns: shell(git push), read(.env), write(src/*.ts), url(https://*.api.com), MyMCP(create_issue)--allow-tool, --deny-tool, ~/.copilot/permissions-config.json, managed permissions.deny, ask, allowno payload logic, no logging, no transformation
preToolUse hookany call the script can recognize in the payload, with a reason; can rewrite arguments.github/hooks, policy.d, plugins, SDKtimeouts fail open; MCP tool naming undocumented
permissionRequest hookthe request before rules and approvals; can interrupt the agentCLI onlynot in the cloud agent; read and hook kinds skip it
Sandboxwhat a running command can reach on the machine/sandbox, --sandbox, sandbox.userPolicy, MDMunconditional autopilot turns the local sandbox off; a hook cannot pre‑approve a bypass
Cloud firewallnetwork egress from the runnerSettings, Copilot, Internet accessbash traffic only; self‑hosted runners unsupported
Managed permissionsShell(rm -rf *), Domain(*.evil.example), Read(**); deny beats ask beats allowmanaged settings, permissions.disableBypassPermissionsModeapplies to clients that fetch managed settings
Watch outDeny always beats allow, even with --allow-all. Put the non-negotiables in managed permission rules, the context-dependent ones in a preToolUse hook, and the reach limits in the sandbox. One rule per control, never the same rule in three places.

Secrets and prompt injection
Two things hooks can catch that nothing else in the chain reads.
01
Secrets in payloads
GitHub provides no built-in secret redaction for hooks. Redact ghp_, gho_, ghu_, ghs_, Bearer tokens, --password and --token before any log line or http POST; the tutorial ships the sed patterns.
02
Prompt injection
userPromptSubmitted sees the prompt; the awesome-copilot governance-audit sample scans for ignore previous instructions and similar patterns with GOVERNANCE_LEVEL and BLOCK_ON_THREAT. From files it can log and warn; from the SDK it can rewrite.
03
Tool results
postToolUse sees what the tool returned before the model does: web_fetch content, file contents, MCP results. modifiedResult can strip an injected instruction; additionalContext can warn the model.
04
Subagent output
subagentStop sees the full response of explore, task, review and custom agents; modifiedResponse edits it, block sends it back. The built-in general-purpose agent does not emit these events.
05
Handled prompts
A userPromptSubmitted hook can answer directly with responseContent and skip the model, since May 2026: the place for a canned answer to a banned request.
Watch outInjection defense in hooks is a second line, not the first. The cloud agent already filters hidden characters and limits the branch; hooks add the patterns your organization cares about, and the log that proves they fired.

Where it stopped

ask. No hook runs; the permission service prompts you because shell is not pre-approved. In the cloud agent all tools are pre-approved, so it runs.allow. The preToolUse guard parses the command, matches nothing on its deny list, exits 0 with an empty object; the permission service then asks or allows per your rules.allow. Policy hook logs the call to the SIEM through http, managed rules allow Shell(npm test), the guard passes. Three controls, one line in the audit.ask, then whatever you click. Nothing recognizes the force push as special; a tired approval at 6 pm rewrites main.deny. The guard matches git push --force to main and returns permissionDecisionReason: use a pull request. The reason goes to the agent, which opens a PR instead.deny, twice. Managed permissions deny Shell(git push --force*) before the hook runs; the policy hook would deny anyway and logs the attempt with the session id.allow. Edits are usually pre-approved; nothing checks the path. Fine on most days.ask. The guard sees edit on src/payments and returns ask with a reason; you approve with the diff in front of you. In the cloud agent ask is deny, so the agent is told to propose the change in the PR body instead.deny. Managed rules put src/payments/** under Edit deny for agents; the policy hook logs the attempt. The change goes through a human.ask for the URL, then fetch. Whatever is on that page reaches the model unread by anything but the model.allow, then postToolUse strips a line that says ignore previous instructions and adds additionalContext: content from an untrusted host. The model sees the page and the warning.deny. Managed permissions deny Domain(pastebin.example); the request never leaves. The policy hook records the attempted URL.

  
Watch outDidactic simulation. The real chain also has the sandbox, the cloud firewall and folder trust. The rule that survives: put the non-negotiable in the control the developer cannot edit, and let the hook explain the why.

Scenarios
Guardrails teams ship first, and the incident each one prevented.
01
Force push to main
preToolUse deny on git push --force to protected branches; the reason tells the agent to open a PR. Rulesets already block it server-side; the hook saves the round trip.
02
Secrets in the shell
Deny curl piped to bash and any command carrying a token flag; log the redacted attempt. The SIEM sees a pattern before a person does.
03
The payments folder
ask on edits under src/payments and deny in the cloud; the reviewer sees every touch with a diff, never a surprise.
04
Untrusted web content
postToolUse on web_fetch strips instruction-like lines and tags the result as untrusted. Cheap, and it fires on every fetch, including subagents'.
Watch outEvery deny needs a reason written for the agent, not for the log. A deny with a bad reason produces a retry loop; a deny with a good reason produces a pull request.

Scene · the finish line
The agent wants to stop. The hook says: not before the tests.
block forces one more turnagentStop returns decision block with a reason; the runtime starts a new turn with that reason as the prompt. Eight blocks maximum.
stop_hook_active is the memoryOn the forced turn the flag is true. Check it first, or your hook blocks the same stop forever and the CLI ends the turn anyway.
Proof, then stopThe hook reads the test log, not the model. When the log says pass, decision allow, and the session ends with evidence.

postToolUse patterns
After every successful tool call: format, lint, fix, annotate.
Format
Prettier after edits
The VS Code quick start: PostToolUse runs npx prettier --write on edited files. The agent never argues about style again, and the diff stays clean.
Lint and links
Fix what the tool just broke
awesome-copilot ships fix-broken-links and dependency-license-checker as postToolUse hooks; run the linter on the touched file and hand the findings back as additionalContext.
Annotate
Tell the model what it cannot see
additionalContext after a tool is joined from all hooks with a blank line and capped at 10 KB: coverage numbers, the owner of the file, the ticket the change belongs to.
Success onlypostToolUse fires only after success; failures go to postToolUseFailure with the error string, where exit 2 stdout becomes context for the retry.
modifiedResultReplace what the model will read: trim a huge log, redact a secret, or set resultType failure to route the call to the failure hook on purpose.
Subagents tooSince May 2026 hooks fire for subagent tool calls; the formatter runs inside a fleet without extra configuration.
Watch outKeep postToolUse hooks idempotent and fast: they run on every call, in fleets on every worker. A ten second linter on every edit turns a two minute task into twenty.

How to · agentStop enforcement
Do not stop until the tests ran. Then stop.
.github/hooks/scripts/stop-guard.sh
#!/usr/bin/env bash                       # .github/hooks/stop.json → agentStop → this scriptINPUT=$(cat)ACTIVE=$(echo "$INPUT" | jq -r '.stop_hook_active')[ "$ACTIVE" = true ] && exit 0                # already forced once: let it stopif ! grep -q "npm test" logs/tool-results.jsonl; then  jq -n '{decision:"block", reason:"Run npm test -- --changed before finishing and report the result."}'  exit 0fijq -n '{decision:"allow"}'# runtime guard: after 8 consecutive blocks the CLI ends the turn anyway# cloud agent: each forced turn counts against the 59 minute job
agentStop fires when the agent wants to end the turn with stopReason end_turn and stop_hook_active telling you whether this turn was already forced by a block. Return decision block with a reason and the runtime starts another turn with that reason as the prompt. After eight consecutive blocks the CLI ends the turn anyway; use stop_hook_active to stop after one forced turn.
In the cloud
Blocks count against the 59 minute job; a block that asks for a full test suite on a slow runner can end the session by timeout. Ask for the fast tests.
Subagents
subagentStop has the same decision plus modifiedResponse; block beats modifiedResponse; the built-in general-purpose agent does not emit it.

Subagents and fleets
Hooks around workers: who emits what, and what you can change.
Who emits
explore, task, code-review, rubber-duck, research, security-review and custom agents emit subagentStart and subagentStop; the built-in general‑purpose agent does not.
subagentStart
Input transcriptPath, agentName, agentDisplayName, agentDescription; output additionalContext prepended to the subagent prompt. Cannot block creation; matcher on agentName.
subagentStop
Input agentId, agentType, agentName, the full response; output decision, reason, modifiedResponse. Last hook wins on modifiedResponse; block beats it and sends the worker back.
Tool calls inside workers
preToolUse and postToolUse fire for subagent tool calls since May 2026; hook.start and hook.end events from subagents are re-emitted on the parent trace since August.
Fleet cost
Every worker runs your hooks. A slow hook is multiplied by the fan-out; a deny with a bad reason loops in N contexts at once.
Watch outUse subagentStop to enforce the contract per worker, a test per module or a schema for the returned summary, and agentStop for the whole. Two gates, two granularities.

One http entry on the events that matter, headers from environment variables, https only.

The enterprise audit log does not include client session data such as local prompts; the docs say some companies use custom hooks to send GitHub Copilot CLI events to their own logging service. An http hook POSTs the payload as JSON to an https URL with headers you set; allowedEnvVars names the variables that may be expanded in headers. localhost only with COPILOT_HOOK_ALLOW_LOCALHOST=1.
Fail-open
Network error, timeout or a non-2xx let the run continue. For evidence that is fine; for a deny it is not, so keep the deny in a command hook and the shipping in http.
Cloud
The sandbox file system is gone at the end; the reference says to retain hook output through an http entry to an allow‑listed host.

OpenTelemetry
Every hook is a span event. Every session is a trace.
01
Span events
github.copilot.hook.start, hook.end and hook.error with github.copilot.hook.type, hook.invocation_id and hook.error_message, on the session span.
02
traceparent
Since August 27, 2026 the hook input carries traceparent and tracestate, and command hooks get them as environment variables: your script can join the trace.
03
Subagents
Hook events from subagent hooks are re-emitted on the parent, so a fleet is one trace with N worker spans and their hooks.
04
Compaction
github.copilot.session.compaction_start and complete, gen_ai.conversation.compacted=true; preCompact fires before both, manual or auto at 95 percent.
05
Where to send it
The telemetry block in managed settings sets the OTLP endpoint for every client; Application Insights or any OTLP collector, joined with Foundry traces by trace id.
06
What it proves
That the guardrail ran, how long it took, and whether it errored. The audit log proves what the agent did on GitHub; the trace proves what your hooks did on the way.
Watch outA guardrail without a span is a claim. Turn OTLP on before the first policy hook, so the day someone asks whether the deny fired, the answer is a query.

Notifications
The async event: wake a person, or wake the session.
GitHub Copilot · payments-apipermission_prompt: git push to main
GitHub Copilot · payments-apiagent_idle: next item from the queue
GitHub Copilot · payments-apishell_completed: npm test, 42 passed
GuardrailsagentStop: PR #128 opened, checks running
The notification event
CLI only, fire-and-forget. Input hook_event_name Notification, message, title and notification_type: shell_completed, shell_detached_completed, agent_completed, agent_idle, permission_prompt, elicitation_dialog. Matcher on notification_type. Output additionalContext is injected as a user message and can wake an idle session.
Human notifications
The docs ship an agentStop and sessionEnd sample: on macOS osascript plays a sound and shows a dialog; on Windows a MessageBox through System.Windows.Forms. From there it is one line to Teams or Slack through an http hook, with the session id in the message.
permission_promptFire a desktop notification when the agent is waiting on you; the cheapest fix for a fleet that stalls at approvals.
agent_idleInject additionalContext to hand the idle session its next item from a queue file. Careful: this is an autopilot you built yourself.
Not in the cloudThe cloud agent never fires notification; the Agents tab, mobile and Slack or Teams carry that role there.

Scenarios
Evidence that answered a question nobody could answer before.
What did the agent run on that laptop
postToolUse http hook to Sentinel with redacted commands and the session id; the audit log had only the PR, the hook had the path.
Did the guardrail fire
hook.end span with the deny reason, queried by invocation id; the ticket closed with a trace link instead of a screenshot.
Which fleet worker touched prod config
Subagent hook events re-emitted on the parent trace; one query, one agentName, one file.
Why did the cloud session time out
agentStop blocks counted against the job timeout; the http hook shipped each block reason, the fix was a faster test target.
Watch outDesign the evidence for the question you will be asked, not for completeness. Three fields, session id, tool and decision, answer most incidents; the payload is there when you need more.

Policy hooks
Admin-installed, loaded first, immune to disableAllHooks.
Where
/etc/github-copilot/policy.d/*.json or C:\ProgramData\GitHub\Copilot\policy.d\*.json, alphabetical, plus the Windows registry HKLM\Software\Policies\GitHub\Copilot with a Policy string holding the JSON.
Integrity
POSIX files must be root-owned and not group or world writable; otherwise they are ignored. Ship them with the MDM, never with the repository.
Behavior
Run regardless of folder trust, in every session, first. disableAllHooks does not touch them. Timeouts still fail open, so keep them fast and local.
Scope
CLI only. The cloud agent reads .github/hooks on the default branch instead; protect that path with a push rule and a ruleset.
With managed settings
allowManagedHooksOnly loads only enterprise-managed hooks and force-enabled plugin hooks; strictPluginOnlyCustomization limits skills, agents, hooks and MCP to plugins. Most restrictive wins.
Watch outA policy hook is a control only if the developer cannot edit the script it calls. Put the script under the same root-owned directory, or inline the logic in the JSON entry with exec and args.

Managed settings and permissions
The keys an enterprise sets once, for every client.
01
allowManagedHooksOnly
only managed hooks and force-enabled plugin hooks load   managed-settings.json, MDM or server   re-fetched hourly; most restrictive wins
02
strictPluginOnlyCustomization
true, or a list of skills, agents, hooks, mcp that must come from plugins   same   pairs with enabledPlugins and strictKnownMarketplaces
03
permissions.deny · ask · allow
Shell(rm -rf *), Domain(*.evil.example), Read(**); deny beats ask beats allow; unmatched asks   same   families Bash or Shell, PowerShell, Read, Edit or Write, Domain
04
permissions.disableBypassPermissionsMode
disable, or allow-auto-only   same   keeps --allow-all from bypassing rules
05
disableAllHooks
skips that file, or every non-policy hook for the repo   hooks file or repository settings.json   the documented switch; no environment variable
06
ChatHooks · ChatAllowManagedHooksOnly
enable hooks in the local harness; managed only   VS Code enterprise policy   plus ChatStrictPluginOnlyCustomization

Hooks in plugins
Package the policy with the skills and the MCP servers it protects.
1
Layout
com.github.copilot/hooks/hooks.json in an Agent Plugin; Claude format in hooks/hooks.json with ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}; Copilot format hooks.json at the root. Nested matcher plus hooks entries are accepted.
2
Variables
CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR, CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA, PLUGIN_ROOT, COPILOT_PLUGIN_ROOT, CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT; templates {{project_dir}} and {{plugin_data_dir}} in entries.
3
Portability
Hooks are not portable across vendors like skills are; the vendor folder exists for that reason. Keep the script logic shared, the entry per client.
4
Control
enabledPlugins forces a plugin on; strictKnownMarketplaces limits sources; strictPluginOnlyCustomization makes plugins the only hook source.
PatternA platform plugin ships the guard, the SIEM hook, the formatter and the skills for the internal tools; one install, one policy.
Load orderPlugins load last; a plugin hook adds to repository and user hooks, never replaces them. Deny wins across all.
UpdatesautoUpdate in managed settings; hook changes reach laptops with the plugin, not with a repository push.
Watch outA plugin is the right vehicle for hooks that protect the plugin's own tools. Organization-wide guardrails still belong in policy hooks and managed permissions, where a developer cannot uninstall them.

Agentic Workflows
In CI the guardrail is not a hook. It is the compiler.
Hooks in a session
Run inside the agent process, see every payload, decide per call, fail open on timeout. The right tool when a person or a cloud agent session is driving.
Safe outputs in a workflow
The agent job has a read-only token; writes go through a separate safe outputs job with caps; a threat detection job scans proposals; the Agent Workflow Firewall limits network. gh aw compile hardens the lock.yml; gh aw audit replays a run.
Same questionsWhat may it call, what may it write, what evidence remains. Hooks answer them in the session; the frontmatter answers them in CI.
Same evidencegh aw logs and gh aw audit RUN-ID are the session log of a workflow; ship them the same way you ship hook output.
Hand-offA workflow's assign-to-agent starts a cloud agent session, and that session reads .github/hooks on the default branch. The two controls meet there.
Watch outDo not port the hooks folder into a workflow. Declare permissions, safe outputs and network in the frontmatter, and keep the hooks for the session the workflow hands off to.

Scenarios
Governance shapes that survived an audit.
01
Bank desktop
Policy hooks in policy.d with a deny script under the same root-owned directory; allowManagedHooksOnly; OTLP to the SIEM. Developers keep formatting hooks in their own folder.
02
Cloud-only org
.github/hooks on main protected by a push rule; the firewall allows the SIEM host; every task's hook output ships by http before the sandbox dies.
03
Platform plugin
The internal MCP servers, their skills and the hooks that gate them in one plugin, forced on by enabledPlugins, updated by autoUpdate.
04
Mixed tooling
A Claude-format hooks file in .claude/settings.json read by three clients; managed permissions carry the non-negotiables so the dialect never matters.
Watch outThe auditor's question is always the same: show me the control the developer cannot change. Policy hooks, managed permissions and push rules are the three answers; everything else is convenience.

Anti-patterns
Six ways a hooks program fails, and the fix for each.
01
Slow guardrail
Times out, fails open, nobody notices. Fix: local deny, http only for shipping evidence.
network call in preToolUse
02
Deny without a reason
The agent retries the same call. Fix: write the reason as the instruction you want followed.
empty permissionDecisionReason
03
Matcher as the only check
The deny never runs in the IDE. Fix: validate the payload in the script.
VS Code ignores it
04
Secrets in the log
The audit trail becomes the leak. Fix: sed the token patterns before every write or POST.
no redaction
05
Hooks only on laptops
The cloud agent runs with no guardrails. Fix: .github/hooks on main, protected by a push rule.
nothing on the default branch
06
Policy in a repository
A control that is a suggestion. Fix: policy.d, managed permissions, allowManagedHooksOnly.
developer can edit it
Watch outMeasure false denies per week and hook latency p95. When either rises, look for one of these six before adding another hook.

The ninety day path
From the first banner to policy hooks in three months.
w1w2w3w4w5w6w7w8w9w10w11w12w13
Days 1 to 30 · observe and guardstarter kit · deny reasons
Days 31 to 60 · automate and shipformatter · tests · SIEM
Days 61 to 90 · governpolicy · managed permissions
GA onlyStarter kit in the top repositories, hooks on the default branch for the cloud agent, /env checks in onboarding, deny reasons written as instructions, OTLP endpoint set. Metric: false denies per week.
adds preview surfaces, labeledFormatter and linter on postToolUse, tests on agentStop, state injection on sessionStart, subagentStop contracts for fleets, http hook to the SIEM with redaction, a platform plugin with the hooks for the internal tools. Metric: hook latency p95 on preToolUse.
operating modelPolicy hooks through the MDM, managed permissions with deny, ask and allow, allowManagedHooksOnly on regulated machines, push rules on .github/hooks, Agentic Workflows frontmatter aligned with the same rules, the six KPIs on one page. Metric: controls the developer cannot change.
Watch outDo not start with policy hooks. Start with a banner and a log, so the first deny arrives in a program people already trust.
